entries.question: What is a star?
alternatives: How does a star work?
What makes a star shine?
entries.answer: A star is an enormous ball of hot gas held together by gravity. For most of a star's life, nuclear fusion deep inside releases the energy that makes it shine. Our Sun is one of billions of stars in the Milky Way.
entries.fact_check: Preserved the definition and solar example. Limited active fusion to the long-lived phase so the line also fits a library that covers stellar remnants.

entries.question: Why do stars have different colours?
alternatives: Why are some stars blue and others red?
What determines a star's colour?
entries.answer: Mostly their surface temperature. The hottest stars appear blue or blue-white, while cooler stars glow orange or red. It's rather fascinating that a star's colour can tell us so much about it.
entries.fact_check: Retained the spoken answer verbatim. Surface temperature is the principal factor in the intrinsic colour trend.

entries.question: What are stellar spectral classes?
alternatives: What do O, B, A, F, G, K and M mean?
How are stellar spectra classified?
entries.answer: They're a way of classifying stars by the patterns in their light, which tell us about their temperatures. O-type stars are the hottest, while M-type stars are the coolest of the main sequence. Our Sun belongs to class G.
entries.fact_check: Retained the spoken answer verbatim. Read O–M in the context of the conventional sequence. Luminosity classes are covered in AST-028. The O to M sequence is ordered from hot to cool.

entries.question: What is an O-type star?
alternatives: Tell me about O-class stars.
What makes O-type stars special?
entries.answer: O-type stars are among the hottest. On the main sequence they're also among the most massive, shining with blue light and using their fuel so quickly that some live only a few million years.
entries.fact_check: Qualified the mass and lifetime comparison as main sequence. Spectral type alone does not specify evolutionary state.

entries.question: What is a B-type blue-white star?
alternatives: Tell me about B-class stars.
What are B-type stars like?
entries.answer: B-type stars are extremely hot and usually appear blue-white. On the main sequence they're much brighter and more massive than the Sun, and they use up their fuel much sooner.
entries.fact_check: Kept the blue-white topic and qualified the mass, brightness and lifetime comparison as main sequence. Removed the colour-only alias because the colour overlaps with neighbouring types.

entries.question: What is an A-type white star?
alternatives: Tell me about A-class stars.
What kind of star is Vega?
entries.answer: A-type stars are hot, bright stars that usually appear white. They're hotter than our Sun, but cooler than the blue giants of classes O and B. Vega is a well-known example.
entries.fact_check: Revised the explanation for accessibility. Vega is a well-known A-type star. The temperature comparison refers to the standard stellar spectral sequence.

entries.question: What is an F-type star?
alternatives: Tell me about F-class stars.
What are F-type stars like?
entries.answer: F-type main-sequence stars are generally a little hotter and more massive than our Sun. They appear white to yellow-white and can remain stable for billions of years. Quite respectable lifetimes, by stellar standards.
entries.fact_check: Scoped mass and lifetime to F-type main-sequence stars. Kept the closing line.

entries.question: What is a G-type star?
alternatives: What type of star is our Sun?
Tell me about G-class stars.
entries.answer: G-type stars include our own Sun. A G-type main-sequence star fuses hydrogen in its core and can shine steadily for billions of years.
entries.fact_check: Kept the solar example. Replaced the claim about life developing with the better supported statement about core fusion and lifetime.

entries.question: What is a K-type star?
alternatives: What is an orange dwarf?
Tell me about K-class stars.
entries.answer: K-type dwarfs are cooler and usually smaller than our Sun, with an orange appearance. Many can shine steadily for tens of billions of years, giving their planetary systems a remarkably long time to evolve.
entries.fact_check: Scoped size and longevity to K dwarfs. K-type spectra also occur in evolved stars.

entries.question: What is an M-type red dwarf?
alternatives: What is a red dwarf?
Tell me about M-class dwarfs.
entries.answer: M-type red dwarfs are small, cool stars and the most common stars in our galaxy. They use their fuel very slowly, and models predict some will shine for trillions of years. An M-type spectrum can belong to a red giant too.
entries.fact_check: Marked trillion-year lifetimes as theoretical and added the distinction between M dwarfs and M giants.

entries.question: What is a brown dwarf?
alternatives: Are brown dwarfs stars?
Why are brown dwarfs different from stars?
entries.answer: A brown dwarf is an object more massive than most planets, but too light to sustain the hydrogen fusion that powers ordinary stars. It gradually cools as it ages and is usually easier to see in infrared light.
entries.fact_check: Kept the sustained hydrogen-fusion criterion and cooling. Replaced the planet-to-star analogy with an infrared observation clue.

entries.question: What are L, T and Y dwarfs?
alternatives: What's the difference between L, T and Y dwarfs?
Tell me about Y-class dwarfs.
entries.answer: These classes describe progressively cooler objects, many of them brown dwarfs. L includes a few very low-mass stars, while T and Y extend to cooler temperatures. These objects are easiest to study in infrared light.
entries.fact_check: Kept the temperature sequence and infrared emphasis. Added the qualification that the warm end of class L includes some very low-mass stars.

entries.question: How are stars born?
alternatives: Where do stars come from?
How does a star form?
entries.answer: Stars begin inside enormous clouds of gas and dust. Gravity pulls some of that material together, making it increasingly hot and dense. If the core gets hot enough for sustained hydrogen fusion, the star enters its main sequence.
entries.fact_check: Distinguished protostar formation and earlier luminosity from the onset of sustained hydrogen burning.

entries.question: What is a protostar?
alternatives: What is a baby star?
Tell me about protostars.
entries.answer: A protostar is a star that's still forming. Gravity is pulling material together and heating it, but stable hydrogen fusion hasn't begun yet. Think of it as a star preparing for its first day on the job.
entries.fact_check: Retained the spoken answer verbatim. Stable hydrogen fusion is the dividing line used here.

entries.question: What is a T Tauri star?
alternatives: Tell me about T Tauri stars.
Are T Tauri stars young?
entries.answer: A T Tauri star is a very young, relatively low-mass star that hasn't settled into its stable adult life yet. Its brightness can change, and it may still be gathering material from its surroundings. A rather restless youngster.
entries.fact_check: Retained the spoken answer verbatim. Accretion is qualified with ‘may’ since it applies in particular to classical T Tauri stars.

entries.question: What is a Herbig Ae/Be star?
alternatives: Tell me about Herbig stars.
How are Herbig stars different from T Tauri stars?
entries.answer: Herbig Ae and Be stars are young stars, generally more massive and hotter than T Tauri stars. They're still approaching their stable adult phase and are often surrounded by gas and dust. Some of that material may eventually form planets.
entries.fact_check: Retained the spoken answer verbatim. The Herbig Ae/Be census supports the mass contrast and disc material.

entries.question: What is a red giant?
alternatives: Why do stars become red giants?
Will our Sun become a red giant?
entries.answer: A red giant is an aging star whose outer layers have expanded enormously after it used up the hydrogen in its core. Its surface becomes cooler and redder, even as the star grows much larger. Our Sun will become one in about five billion years.
entries.fact_check: Retained the spoken answer verbatim. Five billion years is a rounded projection from present-day real-world astronomy.

entries.question: What is a supergiant?
alternatives: What is a red supergiant?
How big are supergiant stars?
entries.answer: Supergiants are exceptionally luminous stars, usually formed as massive stars evolve. Some red supergiants are so enormous that they'd extend beyond the orbit of Mars if placed where our Sun is. Rather inconvenient for the inner planets.
entries.fact_check: Limited the Mars size comparison to red supergiants. Described supergiants by luminosity and evolution without implying that all have the same radius.

entries.question: What is a white dwarf?
alternatives: What remains when a Sun-like star dies?
entries.answer: A white dwarf is the exposed core left after a star like the Sun sheds its outer layers. It can pack over half the Sun's mass into roughly the size of Earth and slowly cools as it radiates away stored heat.
entries.fact_check: Uses the Sun-like evolution pathway. A typical white dwarf is of order Earth's size.

entries.question: What is a supernova?
alternatives: How can a star explode?
entries.answer: A supernova is an enormous stellar explosion. It can happen when a massive star's core collapses, or when a white dwarf undergoes runaway nuclear burning. Either way, the blast can briefly shine brighter than billions of stars.
entries.fact_check: Covers core-collapse and thermonuclear supernovae. Peak luminosities vary.

entries.question: What is a neutron star?
alternatives: What is left when a stellar core collapses into neutron-rich matter?
entries.answer: A neutron star is the compact core some massive stars leave behind when they collapse. It can pack more mass than the Sun into a sphere the size of a city. An exceptionally poor choice of paperweight.
entries.fact_check: NASA's city-scale description refers to diameter and uses approximate masses.

entries.question: What is a pulsar?
alternatives: Why do pulsars pulse?
entries.answer: A pulsar is a spinning neutron star that sends out beams of radiation. If a beam sweeps past us on each rotation, we detect regular pulses, much like seeing the flash of a distant lighthouse.
entries.fact_check: Pulse visibility depends on where the beam points. The compact star is rotating throughout.

entries.question: What is a black hole?
alternatives: How does a black hole trap light?
Tell me about black holes.
entries.answer: A black hole is a region where gravity has curved spacetime so strongly that even light cannot escape from inside its boundary, the event horizon. We can still study black holes through their effects on surrounding matter and light.
entries.fact_check: The event horizon is the boundary for escape to the outside universe. The answer avoids treating the hole as a material surface.

entries.question: What is a Wolf-Rayet star?
alternatives: Why do Wolf-Rayet stars have such strong winds?
entries.answer: Wolf-Rayet stars are very hot stars with powerful winds that give their spectra distinctive bright emission lines. In many massive examples, those winds reveal layers that were once buried beneath the star's outer envelope.
entries.fact_check: Broad emission lines and strong winds define the observational class. The exposed-envelope description is qualified for many massive examples.

entries.question: What is a carbon star?
alternatives: Why are carbon stars so red?
entries.answer: A carbon star has more carbon than oxygen in its outer atmosphere. In many of these stars, carbon produced deeper inside has been mixed up to the surface, where carbon-bearing molecules help give the star a deep red appearance.
entries.fact_check: Sources cover carbon star as described in the linked reference.

entries.question: What is an S-type star?
alternatives: What distinguishes an S star from a carbon star?
entries.answer: An S-type star is a cool giant with distinctive spectral features, including bands from zirconium oxide. In many examples, the atmosphere has nearly as much carbon as oxygen. Its spectrum gives us a glimpse of that unusual chemistry.
entries.fact_check: S-type is a real stellar spectral designation. It is distinct from the unrelated S-type orbital designation.

entries.question: What is a variable star?
alternatives: Why does a star's brightness change?
entries.answer: A variable star changes in apparent brightness over time. Some stars actually brighten and fade as they expand and contract, while others seem to dim when an orbiting companion passes in front.
entries.fact_check: Pulsation is intrinsic variability. Eclipsing binaries exemplify apparent changes from geometry.

entries.question: What is the difference between a giant and a supergiant?
alternatives: How do astronomers tell giants and supergiants apart?
entries.answer: Supergiants are generally more luminous than giants. Astronomers distinguish their luminosity classes using clues in their spectra, including features affected by surface gravity. Colour alone can't tell you which one you're looking at.
entries.fact_check: Luminosity class compares spectral features and is independent of the O–M temperature ordering.

entries.question: What is a binary star system?
alternatives: Can two stars orbit one another?
entries.answer: In a binary system, two stars are held together by gravity and orbit a common centre of mass. Some pairs are so close that one star can transfer material to the other.
entries.fact_check: A binary is gravitationally bound. The transfer example applies to sufficiently close systems.

entries.question: What is a solar flare?
alternatives: Why does the Sun produce flares?
entries.answer: A solar flare is a sudden burst of radiation from the Sun, powered by energy released when magnetic fields rapidly rearrange. Flares can happen on other stars too, where they're called stellar flares.
entries.fact_check: Magnetic energy release produces a radiation burst. A flare and a coronal mass ejection are distinct phenomena.

entries.question: What is a stellar corona?
alternatives: What is the Sun's outer atmosphere?
entries.answer: A corona is a star's outer atmosphere. The Sun's is made of very hot, thin plasma, and you can see it as a pale glow around the Moon during a total solar eclipse.
entries.fact_check: The eclipse example applies to the solar corona. The bright photosphere is blocked by the Moon.

entries.question: What is a stellar jet?
alternatives: Why do some young stars shoot out jets?
entries.answer: A stellar jet is a narrow stream of fast-moving material launched from near a star. Around a young star, jets can shoot out in opposite directions as material from a surrounding disc feeds the star.
entries.fact_check: The source describes a protostellar jet driven by material interacting near the star. The answer is scoped to young stars.

entries.question: What is a planetary nebula?
alternatives: How does a planetary nebula form?
entries.answer: A planetary nebula forms when a dying star like the Sun sheds its outer layers and the exposed hot core makes the gas glow. The name comes from its planet-like appearance in early telescopes. The planets can sit this one out.
entries.fact_check: Ionised gas glows around a hot remnant of a low- or intermediate-mass star. The name describes its historical appearance.

entries.question: What is an exoplanet?
alternatives: What counts as a planet beyond the Solar System?
entries.answer: An exoplanet is a planet beyond our Solar System. Most known examples orbit other stars, and their variety is rather humbling: some are scorched giants and others are rocky worlds closer to Earth's size.
entries.fact_check: Definition and examples from NASA's exoplanet overview.

entries.question: What is a rocky planet?
alternatives: What is a terrestrial planet?
entries.answer: A rocky planet is made mostly of rock and metal, with a solid surface beneath any atmosphere. Mercury, Venus, Earth and Mars are our local examples, and they show how differently rocky worlds can turn out.
entries.fact_check: Rock and metal distinguish terrestrial planets by bulk composition.

entries.question: What is a super-Earth?
alternatives: Does super-Earth mean Earth-like?
entries.answer: A super-Earth is a planet more massive than Earth and less massive than Neptune. That's a description of mass. Its surface, atmosphere and prospects for life are separate questions.
entries.fact_check: Mass category in NASA's exoplanet guide. Composition remains an independent question.

entries.question: What is a gas giant?
alternatives: What are planets like Jupiter made of?
entries.answer: A gas giant is a large planet made mostly of hydrogen and helium. Deeper down, the pressure rises until those familiar gases behave in unfamiliar ways. There is no solid surface like Earth's to stand on.
entries.fact_check: Hydrogen and helium dominate the giant planet. The interior description avoids assigning it a solid surface.

entries.question: What is an ice giant?
alternatives: Why are Uranus and Neptune called ice giants?
entries.answer: Ice giants such as Uranus and Neptune contain a greater proportion of substances like water, ammonia and methane than Jupiter and Saturn do. In planetary science those ingredients are called ices, even when they're hot and under enormous pressure.
entries.fact_check: Water, ammonia and methane are planetary-science ices. Actual states vary with pressure and temperature.

entries.question: What is a hot Jupiter?
alternatives: How close can a gas giant orbit its star?
entries.answer: A hot Jupiter is a gas giant that orbits very close to its star. Many complete an orbit in just a few days, so their years are short and their atmospheres receive an extraordinary amount of starlight.
entries.fact_check: Uses the established close-orbit term and a representative period range.

entries.question: What is a dwarf planet?
alternatives: Why is Pluto called a dwarf planet?
entries.answer: A dwarf planet orbits the Sun directly and is massive enough for gravity to pull it into a nearly round shape. It hasn't cleared its orbital neighbourhood. Pluto is the familiar example out beyond Neptune.
entries.fact_check: Uses the IAU Solar System definition through NASA. ‘Directly’ distinguishes orbiting the Sun from being a satellite.

entries.question: What is an ocean world?
alternatives: Can an ocean exist beneath ice?
entries.answer: An ocean world has a substantial body of liquid, sometimes hidden beneath a crust of ice. Europa and Enceladus are examples where evidence points to subsurface oceans, with energy from tidal flexing helping keep water liquid.
entries.fact_check: NASA ocean-world evidence distinguishes subsurface water from exposed surface oceans.

entries.question: What is the habitable zone?
alternatives: What is the Goldilocks zone?
entries.answer: The habitable zone is the range of distances from a star where a rocky planet with a suitable atmosphere could have liquid water on its surface. It's a good place to look, and the atmosphere still has a great deal to say about the outcome.
entries.fact_check: A surface-water criterion with an atmosphere assumption. Compare PLA-008 for subsurface oceans.

entries.question: What is tidal locking?
alternatives: Why does the Moon keep the same face toward Earth?
entries.answer: An object is tidally locked in synchronous rotation when it spins once in the time it takes to orbit its partner. That keeps the same side facing its companion, as the Moon does with Earth. It still rotates, just in step with its orbit.
entries.fact_check: Sources cover tidal locking as described in the linked reference.

entries.question: What is tidal heating?
alternatives: How can gravity warm a moon?
entries.answer: A moon can flex as the gravitational pull across it changes along its orbit. The repeated squeezing and stretching generates heat inside. On an icy world, that heat can help sustain an ocean beneath the surface.
entries.fact_check: Tidally driven flexing supplies internal heat where changing stresses dissipate energy.

entries.question: What is the greenhouse effect?
alternatives: Why does an atmosphere trap heat?
entries.answer: A greenhouse effect occurs when gases absorb some of the infrared radiation a planet's surface gives off and re-emit it. That leaves the surface warmer than it would otherwise be. Venus shows how powerful this can become.
entries.fact_check: Absorption and emission of infrared radiation describe the greenhouse effect. Venus provides a worked natural example.

entries.question: Why is Venus hotter than Mercury?
alternatives: How is Venus the hottest planet?
entries.answer: Venus has a thick carbon dioxide atmosphere that produces an exceptionally strong greenhouse effect. Mercury orbits closer to the Sun, yet Venus has the hotter surface. Distance from a star is only part of the story.
entries.fact_check: NASA's comparison identifies the thick atmosphere and greenhouse warming as the reason for Venus's higher surface temperature.

entries.question: Why is Mars red?
alternatives: What gives Mars its rusty colour?
entries.answer: Much of the dust on Mars contains iron oxides, the family of compounds that gives rust its colour. Fine dust covers large areas and can spread through the atmosphere, lending the planet its familiar reddish look.
entries.fact_check: NASA describes iron oxidation and widespread dust as the source of the colour.

entries.question: What are planetary rings made of?
alternatives: Are Saturn's rings solid?
entries.answer: Planetary rings are swarms of independently orbiting particles. Saturn's rings consist mainly of water ice with some dust and rock, and the pieces range from tiny grains to much larger chunks.
entries.fact_check: NASA describes mainly ice plus some rock and dust. Individual particles orbit independently.

entries.question: What is an asteroid?
alternatives: What is a minor rocky Solar System body?
entries.answer: Asteroids are small bodies left over from the Solar System's formation. Many are rocky or metallic, and many orbit between Mars and Jupiter. That belt is a broad region of space with ample room between objects.
entries.fact_check: Main-belt location applies to many asteroids. The answer avoids implying a dense obstacle field.

entries.question: Why does a comet grow a tail?
alternatives: Why do comet tails point away from the Sun?
entries.answer: As a comet warms near the Sun, its ices release gas and dust, forming a cloud around the nucleus. Sunlight pushes dust away while the solar wind shapes the ionised gas. The tails point broadly away from the Sun, even when the comet is heading outward.
entries.fact_check: Solar radiation pressure and solar wind act on different material. Direction is approximate, especially for a curved dust tail.

entries.question: What is a rogue planet?
alternatives: Can a planet travel without a star?
entries.answer: A rogue planet travels through space without orbiting a star. One way this can happen is through a gravitational encounter that ejects a planet from its original system. Finding such a faint wanderer takes a little ingenuity.
entries.fact_check: NASA describes ejection as a possible origin. It is presented as one pathway.

entries.question: How does the transit method find planets?
alternatives: Why does a star dim when a planet crosses it?
entries.answer: When a planet crosses in front of its star from our viewpoint, it blocks a little starlight. Repeated dips can reveal the planet's orbital period, and the depth of a dip helps estimate its size if we know the star's size.
entries.fact_check: Depth depends on the fraction of the star's light blocked. The period comes from repeat timing.

entries.question: How does radial velocity reveal a planet?
alternatives: Can a star's wobble reveal a planet?
entries.answer: A planet tugs its star back and forth as they orbit their common centre of mass. That motion shifts the star's spectral lines slightly toward red and blue. The pattern can reveal an unseen planet and help constrain its mass.
entries.fact_check: Doppler shifts measure line-of-sight motion. Inclination can limit the mass inferred.

entries.question: What is an Earth-like World in Elite Dangerous?
alternatives: What does ELW mean in the game?
entries.answer: In Elite Dangerous, Earth-like World is a planet class with a breathable atmosphere and native life. It's a broad classification. Two Earth-like Worlds can still differ in their gravity, temperature and other properties.
entries.fact_check: Frontier Scan event and planet-class appendix. The gameplay label is distinct from a real exoplanet habitability claim.

entries.question: What is a High Metal Content body in Elite Dangerous?
alternatives: What does HMC mean on the system map?
entries.answer: In Elite Dangerous, High Metal Content is a planet class for solid bodies with a substantial metal component. The class describes the body's composition. Surface biology and landing suitability are separate pieces of exploration data.
entries.fact_check: Frontier Scan event and planet-class appendix. Landable, atmosphere and geological or biological signals are independent data.

entries.question: What is an Ammonia World in Elite Dangerous?
alternatives: What does the game's Ammonia World class mean?
entries.answer: An Ammonia World is a planet where ammonia plays a role similar to water on Earth, forming lakes or oceans. In Elite Dangerous, these worlds can even support ammonia-based life. A rather different recipe for a living planet.
entries.fact_check: Describes the in-game Ammonia World classification, including ammonia-rich surface liquids and the possibility of ammonia-based life within Elite Dangerous lore.

entries.question: What is a Water World in Elite Dangerous?
alternatives: What does Water World mean on the system map?
entries.answer: In Elite Dangerous, a Water World is a planet with large amounts of water, often covering much of its surface. Some may be suitable for terraforming, but that depends on more than just the presence of water.
entries.fact_check: Frontier Scan event and planet-class appendix. Planet class and TerraformState are separate values.

entries.question: What is exobiology in Elite Dangerous?
alternatives: How does on-foot biology sampling work?
entries.answer: In Elite Dangerous: Odyssey, exobiology lets you collect biological samples on foot. The Artemis suit carries a Genetic Sampler, and a completed set can be turned in at Vista Genomics. It's a field trip with rather better equipment.
entries.fact_check: The Odyssey guide and sampler record cover the Artemis loadout and Vista Genomics handoff.

entries.question: What is Stratum?
alternatives: What are those low Stratum colonies in Odyssey?
entries.answer: In Odyssey, Stratum is a genus of low-growing organisms that spread in broad patches across the ground. Different species can share that low profile, so the overall shape is a clue to the genus and the sampler can confirm the identification.
entries.fact_check: Codex genus Stratum. Low layered patches are a visual cue. Stratum Tectonicas is one species in this genus.

entries.question: What is Bacterium?
alternatives: What are Bacterium colonies in Odyssey?
entries.answer: In Odyssey, Bacterium is a genus of microbial colonies that can look like flat stains on the ground. Depending on the surface and lighting, they can be easy to miss. Apparently camouflage doesn't require legs.
entries.fact_check: Codex genus Bacterium. Field descriptions support the flat, stain-like forms. Capitalisation distinguishes the game label from the generic noun.

entries.question: What is an Aleoida?
alternatives: What does the Aleoida genus look like?
entries.answer: In Odyssey, Aleoida is a genus with clustered, pointed growths. Some forms look like rosettes. That's a handy visual cue when you're learning the genus, and the Genetic Sampler can settle the identification.
entries.fact_check: Codex genus spelling checked against the species index. Appearance is a broad field cue and varies among species and colour variants.

entries.question: What is Cactoida?
alternatives: What does the Cactoida genus look like?
entries.answer: In Odyssey, Cactoida is a genus with compact, often rounded growths. The name is a useful reminder of its cactus-like appearance. It belongs to the game's own catalogue of alien life.
entries.fact_check: Codex genus spelling checked against the species index. Appearance is a broad field cue and varies among species and colour variants.

entries.question: What is Clypeus?
alternatives: What does the Clypeus genus look like?
entries.answer: In Odyssey, Clypeus is a genus known for broad, shield-like forms. That's the main shape to look for, even when the colour or finer details differ.
entries.fact_check: Codex genus spelling checked against the species index. Appearance is a broad field cue and varies among species and colour variants.

entries.question: What is Concha?
alternatives: What does the Concha genus look like?
entries.answer: In Odyssey, Concha is a genus with curved, shell-like growths. The silhouette is particularly helpful when you're looking over broken terrain.
entries.fact_check: Codex genus spelling checked against the species index. Appearance is a broad field cue and varies among species and colour variants.

entries.question: What is Electricae?
alternatives: What are the glowing Electricae organisms?
entries.answer: In Odyssey, Electricae is a genus of luminous organisms. Its glow is a helpful visual clue when you're exploring in low light. The Genetic Sampler can identify the species.
entries.fact_check: Codex genus spelling checked against the species index. Appearance is a broad field cue and varies among species and colour variants.

entries.question: What is Fonticulua?
alternatives: What does the Fonticulua genus look like?
entries.answer: In Odyssey, Fonticulua is a genus of upright organisms with profiles that can look like mushrooms or branching fountains. The contours vary by species. A pleasing bit of variety for something rooted to the spot.
entries.fact_check: Codex genus spelling checked against the species index. Appearance is a broad field cue and varies among species and colour variants.

entries.question: What is Frutexa?
alternatives: What does the Frutexa genus look like?
entries.answer: In Odyssey, Frutexa is a genus with shrub-like growth. Think of clusters of branching stems close to the ground. The resemblance to a shrub is a visual cue for the game.
entries.fact_check: Codex genus spelling checked against the species index. Appearance is a broad field cue and varies among species and colour variants.

entries.question: What is Fumerola?
alternatives: How is Fumerola different from a fumarole?
entries.answer: Fumerola is a genus of alien organisms found around active volcanic vents. They thrive in environments that would be hostile to many other forms of life. Apparently, some organisms prefer their surroundings rather hot.
entries.fact_check: Describes Fumerola as an Odyssey biological genus associated with volcanic environments. The geological term fumarole is distinct from the biological genus.

entries.question: What is Fungoida?
alternatives: What does the Fungoida genus look like?
entries.answer: In Odyssey, Fungoida is a genus of fungus-like organisms. Their compact growths can be easy to overlook against rocky terrain. The name is a good way to remember the general shape.
entries.fact_check: Codex genus spelling checked against the species index. Appearance is a broad field cue and varies among species and colour variants.

entries.question: What is Osseus?
alternatives: What does the Osseus genus look like?
entries.answer: In Odyssey, Osseus is a genus with hard-looking forms that can blend in among rocks. Its shapes vary, so a promising silhouette is a reason to look closer.
entries.fact_check: Codex genus spelling checked against the species index. Appearance is a broad field cue and varies among species and colour variants.

entries.question: What is Recepta?
alternatives: What is the Recepta genus in Odyssey?
entries.answer: Recepta is a genus of alien life found on planetary surfaces. Its species form unusual, often lattice-like structures that can look almost artificial. Nature does seem rather fond of geometry.
entries.fact_check: Describes the Recepta genus using its distinctive geometric and lattice-like structures. Visual appearance may vary between species and variants.

entries.question: What is Tubus?
alternatives: What does the Tubus genus look like?
entries.answer: In Odyssey, Tubus is a genus of tall, tube-like organisms. The upright profile is a useful clue when you're learning to distinguish the surface genera.
entries.fact_check: Codex genus spelling checked against the species index. Appearance is a broad field cue and varies among species and colour variants.

entries.question: What is Tussock?
alternatives: What are those grass-like Tussock growths?
entries.answer: In Odyssey, Tussock is a genus of tufted, grass-like organisms. Their low clumps can be easier to pick out by shape than by colour alone.
entries.fact_check: Codex genus spelling checked against the species index. Appearance is a broad field cue and varies among species and colour variants.

entries.question: Why does the sampler need three samples?
alternatives: Why is a colony too close to sample?
entries.answer: In Odyssey, the Genetic Sampler needs three sufficiently separated samples of the same species to complete a set. The required separation varies with the organism. If the sampler flags a colony as too close, look farther from the sites you've already sampled.
entries.fact_check: Confirmed same-species three-part sampling and variable separation. Exact distances, scanner ranges and payouts are excluded.

entries.question: What does the biological filter on the DSS show?
alternatives: Does the blue overlay pinpoint a specimen?
entries.answer: In Odyssey, after mapping a body you can switch the Detailed Surface Scanner overlay between available biological filters. The shaded areas guide you toward possible habitat. You'll still need to search the surface for actual specimens.
entries.fact_check: The overlay is a search aid after mapping. It does not promise specimens at a coordinate.

entries.question: What is Vista Genomics?
alternatives: Where do I turn in finished genetic samples?
entries.answer: In Odyssey, Vista Genomics is where you turn in completed genetic samples. Look for its counter in supported station concourses. The staff handle the paperwork, which seems fair after all that walking.
entries.fact_check: The Odyssey guide documents the Vista Genomics turn-in. Payouts and service availability are build-sensitive.

entries.question: What is a biosignature?
alternatives: What might count as evidence of alien life?
entries.answer: A biosignature is a possible sign of life, such as a chemical pattern that living organisms might produce. Scientists also look for non-living processes that could make the same signal. One intriguing clue is usually the beginning of the investigation.
entries.fact_check: NASA discusses false positives from non-biological processes. A candidate signal requires corroboration.

entries.question: What is an extremophile?
alternatives: Can life live under extreme conditions?
entries.answer: An extremophile is an organism that thrives in conditions many other organisms would find harsh, such as intense heat, acidity or salinity. Studying these organisms on Earth helps us think about which environments could support life elsewhere.
entries.fact_check: NASA Astrobiology describes Earth organisms thriving across extremes. Applicability beyond Earth is an inference.

entries.question: What is astrobiology?
alternatives: What do real scientists mean by exobiology?
entries.answer: Astrobiology studies life's origins, evolution and prospects across the universe. That includes learning from life on Earth and working out how we might recognise evidence of life elsewhere. It's part biology, part astronomy and very much a team effort.
entries.fact_check: NASA's programme defines the field broadly. Its research covers Earth life and the search beyond Earth.

entries.question: What kind of galaxy is the Milky Way?
alternatives: Is the Milky Way a barred spiral?
entries.answer: The Milky Way is a barred spiral galaxy. It has a flat disc with spiral arms and a bar of stars through its central region. From inside that disc, much of the galaxy appears as a band across our sky.
entries.fact_check: NASA and ESA identify the Milky Way as a barred spiral with a disc and arms.

entries.question: What is a galactic spiral arm?
alternatives: Are stars trapped in spiral arms?
entries.answer: A spiral arm is a curved structure in a galaxy's disc, often traced by young stars and clouds of gas. The arms are patterns in the disc, and individual stars can move relative to them.
entries.fact_check: The cited spiral-arm study models stars moving relative to arm structure. The answer makes no universal claim about how arms form.

entries.question: Where is the Sun in the Milky Way?
alternatives: What is the Orion Spur?
entries.answer: The Sun sits in the Milky Way's disc, in a small structure called the Orion Spur, between the Sagittarius and Perseus arms. It's about twenty-six thousand light-years from the Galactic Centre. A suburban address, as galaxies go.
entries.fact_check: NASA and ESA place the Sun in the local spur; galactocentric distance is rounded.

entries.question: What is the galactic bulge?
alternatives: What is the dense middle of a spiral galaxy?
entries.answer: The bulge is a dense central concentration of stars. In the Milky Way it rises above and below the flatter disc, and the central bar helps shape it. It spans a region far larger than the black hole at the centre.
entries.fact_check: ESA describes the central stellar bulge and bar within the disc.

entries.question: What is a galactic halo?
alternatives: What surrounds the Milky Way's disc?
entries.answer: The Milky Way's stellar halo is a sparse, extended population of stars and clusters around the disc. A more massive halo of dark matter also surrounds the visible galaxy. We infer the latter largely through its gravitational effects.
entries.fact_check: Distinguishes the observed stellar population from the inferred dark matter halo.

entries.question: What is the Galactic Centre?
alternatives: What lies at the centre of the Milky Way?
entries.answer: The Galactic Centre is the Milky Way's crowded central region, rich in stars, gas and dust. The supermassive black hole Sagittarius A-star sits at its heart. Infrared and radio observations can reveal features that dust hides from visible-light telescopes.
entries.fact_check: NASA Webb describes the observationally crowded central region. Compare LOC-001 for the black hole itself.

entries.question: What is the galactic plane?
alternatives: What does above the galactic disc mean?
entries.answer: The galactic plane is the reference plane along the middle of the Milky Way's disc. It gives us a way to describe how far above or below the disc something lies. The disc itself has thickness, so the plane is a useful reference.
entries.fact_check: The midplane is a reference within an extended, finite-thickness disc.

entries.question: What is the interstellar medium?
alternatives: Is the space between stars empty?
entries.answer: The interstellar medium is the gas and dust between stars. Some of it is cold enough to form dense clouds, and some is extremely hot and diffuse. Empty space turns out to have quite a range of working conditions.
entries.fact_check: Interstellar material includes both diffuse gas and colder clouds. Temperature examples stay qualitative.

entries.question: What is a molecular cloud?
alternatives: Where can interstellar molecules gather?
entries.answer: A molecular cloud is a cold interstellar cloud where much of the hydrogen is in molecular form. Dense pockets can collapse under gravity and form stars. The dust also makes parts of a cloud hard to see in visible light.
entries.fact_check: Cold molecular hydrogen clouds contain dense regions that can form stars.

entries.question: What is a dark nebula?
alternatives: Why do some nebulae look like holes in the sky?
entries.answer: A dark nebula is a cloud whose dust blocks visible light from stars or glowing gas behind it. Its silhouette can make it look like a gap in the sky. Infrared observations can sometimes show what the dust conceals.
entries.fact_check: Hubble distinguishes dark nebulae by the light blocked by their dust.

entries.question: What is an open star cluster?
alternatives: Why are some young stars grouped together?
entries.answer: An open cluster is a group of stars that formed from the same cloud. Open clusters are typically looser and younger than globular clusters. Over time, interactions with other objects in the galaxy can scatter their members.
entries.fact_check: NASA contrasts typical open and globular clusters by age and structure. Open-cluster dispersal is gradual.

entries.question: What is a globular cluster?
alternatives: What are those dense round star clusters?
entries.answer: A globular cluster is a tightly bound, roughly spherical group of stars. Many in the Milky Way contain very old stars and orbit in the halo. They give astronomers a glimpse of the galaxy's early history.
entries.fact_check: Old stars and a spherical, bound distribution are characteristic. Halo membership is qualified.

entries.question: What is a light-year?
alternatives: Is a light-year a distance or a time?
entries.answer: A light-year is the distance light travels in vacuum in one year. It's about nine and a half trillion kilometres. The name sounds like a calendar entry, but it belongs on a map.
entries.fact_check: The distance assumes light propagation in vacuum. The kilometre conversion is rounded.

entries.question: What is a parsec?
alternatives: How many light-years are in a parsec?
entries.answer: A parsec is about three and a quarter light-years. The unit comes from parallax, the tiny apparent shift of nearby stars against the background as Earth changes position in its orbit.
entries.fact_check: A parsec comes from parallax and equals approximately 3.26 light-years.

entries.question: What is the Local Group?
alternatives: Which group of galaxies includes the Milky Way?
entries.answer: The Local Group is the collection of nearby galaxies that includes the Milky Way, Andromeda, Triangulum and many smaller galaxies. It's our neighbourhood on a scale where whole galaxies count as neighbours.
entries.fact_check: NASA's group description includes the three named major members and smaller galaxies.

entries.question: What are Galactic Regions in Elite Dangerous?
alternatives: How does the game divide the galaxy for the Codex?
entries.answer: In Elite Dangerous, the galaxy is divided into forty-two named regions. The Codex organises exploration records by these regions, so the boundary can affect where an entry is filed.
entries.fact_check: The Codex uses named game regions. The map breakdown gives the count of 42.

entries.question: What is the Bubble in Elite Dangerous?
alternatives: What does the inhabited Bubble mean?
entries.answer: In Elite Dangerous, the Bubble is the main expanse of inhabited human space around Sol. The name describes a broad region with many settled systems and stations. Human settlements also exist far beyond it.
entries.fact_check: EDSM usage identifies the Bubble as the main inhabited region near Sol. No fixed political boundary is claimed.

entries.question: What is the Colonia region?
alternatives: What does Colonia mean as a destination in Elite Dangerous?
entries.answer: In Elite Dangerous, Colonia is both the name of a system and a name for the surrounding region of human settlement. It's far from the main Bubble and a familiar destination on long-distance exploration routes.
entries.fact_check: EDSM records Colonia and long-distance routes from the Bubble. The answer distinguishes system from region.

entries.question: What is Sagittarius A*?
alternatives: What is Sag A-star?
Tell me about Sagittarius A-star.
entries.answer: In astronomy, Sagittarius A-star is the supermassive black hole at the centre of the Milky Way, with about four million times the Sun's mass. Elite Dangerous makes it a visitable destination. The real one is best admired by telescope.
entries.fact_check: ESO/EHT supplies the real black hole and rounded mass. EDSM supplies the visitable game destination.

entries.question: What is Beagle Point?
alternatives: Why is Beagle Point an exploration landmark?
entries.answer: In Elite Dangerous, Beagle Point is a remote system on the far side of the galaxy from Sol. Explorers know it as the destination of the original Distant Worlds expedition. It makes a fitting place to pause and look back.
entries.fact_check: Sources cover Beagle Point as an in-game classification, mechanic or recorded location.

entries.question: What is the Great Annihilator?
alternatives: What is the Great Annihilator in Elite Dangerous?
entries.answer: In Elite Dangerous, Great Annihilator is a named black-hole system toward the Galactic Centre. The name comes from a real X-ray source that astronomers interpret as a likely black-hole binary.
entries.fact_check: EDSM records the named game system. NASA Swift catalogues the real candidate 1E 1740.7−2942. Game body properties are excluded.

entries.question: What is Explorer's Anchorage?
alternatives: Which station is close to Sagittarius A-star in Elite Dangerous?
entries.answer: In Elite Dangerous, Explorer's Anchorage is a station in Stuemeae FG-Y d7561, near Sagittarius A-star. Its name is a small kindness to anyone who has just crossed half the galaxy.
entries.fact_check: EDSM associates the station with Stuemeae FG-Y d7561 near the Galactic Centre. No services or live availability are asserted.

entries.question: What is the Orion Nebula?
alternatives: What is Messier 42?
entries.answer: The Orion Nebula is a cloud of glowing gas and dust where stars are forming. Ultraviolet light from young stars makes some of the surrounding gas shine. We can see the nebula from Earth in the region of Orion's sword.
entries.fact_check: Hubble identifies the Orion Nebula as an emission nebula and nearby star-forming region.

entries.question: What are the Pillars of Creation?
alternatives: Where are the Pillars of Creation?
entries.answer: The Pillars of Creation are columns of gas and dust in the Eagle Nebula. Radiation from nearby young stars erodes their surfaces. Infrared images can show stars within and around the pillars that visible light struggles to reveal.
entries.fact_check: Hubble compares visible and infrared views of the Eagle Nebula pillars and explains erosion by nearby stars.

entries.question: What is the Crab Nebula?
alternatives: What did the supernova of 1054 leave behind?
entries.answer: The Crab Nebula is the expanding remnant of a supernova observed in 1054. A pulsar at its centre supplies energy to the surrounding nebula. The original flash has faded, but the remnant is still luminous.
entries.fact_check: Hubble identifies the historical 1054 supernova, pulsar and energetic surrounding remnant.

entries.question: What are the Pleiades?
alternatives: What are the Seven Sisters in astronomy?
entries.answer: The Pleiades are a nearby open cluster of young stars, also called the Seven Sisters. The blue haze in deep images is dust reflecting starlight. The cluster itself contains many more stars than the familiar handful we see easily.
entries.fact_check: Hubble's M45 catalogue describes the star cluster and dusty reflection nebulosity.

entries.question: What is Proxima Centauri?
alternatives: Which star is closest to the Sun?
entries.answer: Proxima Centauri is a red dwarf just over four light-years away and the nearest star to the Sun. Even at that distance it's too faint for the unaided eye. It occasionally brightens in flares.
entries.fact_check: Hubble identifies the nearest stellar neighbour and its flares. Distance is rounded.

entries.question: What is Betelgeuse?
alternatives: What kind of star is Betelgeuse?
entries.answer: Betelgeuse is a red supergiant in Orion. Its brightness varies, and during its famous dimming a dust cloud helped obscure the star. A striking change in brightness can tell us a great deal about a star's outer layers.
entries.fact_check: Hubble reports a cloud of dust as a contributor to the dimming episode. No explosion date is implied.

entries.question: What is TRAPPIST-1?
alternatives: Why is the TRAPPIST-1 planet system interesting?
entries.answer: TRAPPIST-1 is a small, cool star orbited by seven known planets roughly the size of Earth. Astronomers can watch them transit the star to learn about their sizes and investigate whether they have atmospheres.
entries.fact_check: NASA discusses the seven known transiting planets. Atmospheres remain under study.

entries.question: What is the Andromeda Galaxy?
alternatives: What is Messier 31?
entries.answer: Andromeda is a large spiral galaxy in the Local Group, about two and a half million light-years away. Under dark skies it can look like a faint smudge. That's a whole galaxy's worth of stars in a rather modest patch of sky.
entries.fact_check: Hubble's M31 catalogue supports the galaxy type and rounded distance.

entries.question: What are the Magellanic Clouds?
alternatives: Are the Magellanic Clouds galaxies?
entries.answer: The Large and Small Magellanic Clouds are nearby dwarf galaxies visible from the southern sky. Their cloudy appearance comes from the combined light of many stars, and their gas contains regions where new stars are forming.
entries.fact_check: NASA identifies the two dwarf galaxies and their visible stellar and gas components.

entries.question: What is a Lagrange point?
alternatives: How can an object keep its position relative to two orbiting bodies?
entries.answer: A Lagrange point is a location in a system of two orbiting bodies where a small third object can keep the same relative position as it moves with them. Some of these locations are more stable than others, which matters when choosing a place for a spacecraft.
entries.fact_check: Uses the restricted three-body interpretation. Stability depends on the point and system.

entries.question: What is a Lagrange Cloud in Elite Dangerous?
alternatives: What can a Lagrange Cloud contain in the game?
entries.answer: In Elite Dangerous, Lagrange Clouds are encounters in space that can contain crystals and unusual lifeforms. Some are catalogued as storm clouds. A visit is a chance to inspect the particular phenomena recorded there.
entries.fact_check: Canonn maps the in-game encounters and storm-cloud subclass. See LOC-014 for the real orbital concept.

entries.question: What is a Notable Stellar Phenomenon in Elite Dangerous?
alternatives: What does an NSP signal mean?
entries.answer: In Elite Dangerous, a Notable Stellar Phenomenon is a signal in space you can investigate. Such encounters can include unusual minerals, lifeforms or anomalies. The signal label is an invitation to look closer, and the findings can go in the Codex.
entries.fact_check: Canonn records classes of space encounters and Frontier documents Codex records. No encounter is promised at a given location.

entries.question: What are Guardian ruins?
alternatives: What are Guardian Ancient Ruins in Elite Dangerous?
entries.answer: In Elite Dangerous, Guardian ruins are archaeological sites left by an alien civilisation. Canonn's surveys record recurring layouts and locations across multiple systems. They're a chance to investigate the Guardians through what they left behind.
entries.fact_check: Canonn's ruin survey lists sites and recurring layouts. No invented Guardian events are included.

entries.question: What are Crystalline Shards in Elite Dangerous?
alternatives: What are the game's surface Crystalline Shards?
entries.answer: In Elite Dangerous, Crystalline Shards are catalogued surface growths that look like clusters of crystals. They're a separate encounter from the crystals found in Lagrange Clouds. Same eye for decoration, different address.
entries.fact_check: Canonn lists the surface category separately from cloud crystals. Mineral appearance serves as a visual cue.

entries.question: What are Thargoid Barnacles?
alternatives: What are the large barnacle formations in Elite Dangerous?
entries.answer: In Elite Dangerous, Thargoid Barnacles are alien formations found at surface sites. Canonn surveys catalogue those sites across planets and moons. The in-game name describes a Thargoid feature and its appearance is quite distinct from an Earth barnacle.
entries.fact_check: Canonn records Thargoid Barnacles as distinct surface sites. The biology comparison is limited to ordinary appearance.
